title: Hall, yard and zones overview
text:
1. The Harborwick site centres on a single warehouse hall covering 6,000 m2, with an adjoining outdoor yard for manoeuvring and parking. Learn the hall perimeter, the yard entrances and the marked internal routes before starting work.
2. Eight dock doors serve the building on one facade. Dock doors 1-4 are assigned to inbound receiving, while dock doors 5-8 are assigned to outbound dispatch, including 4 outbound dock doors available for loading.
3. Zone A forms the receiving zone at inbound docks 1-4. All unloading and goods inspection takes place there, and inbound vehicles are marshalled to those four doors only.
4. From Zone A, approved stock moves directly into storage. Zone B provides bulk storage in high-bay pallet racking, which offers 2,400 pallet positions across the high bays.
5. Zone C operates as the picking zone. It contains ground-level pick faces and flow racks arranged for short travel and scanner-directed work, separate from the high-bay reserve in Zone B.
6. Zone D provides the dispatch zone for outbound staging in front of docks 5-8. Build and check outbound loads there, keeping each door apron clear for the next trailer.
7. Zone E is the cold zone for chilled storage held at +2 to +6 °C. Access is restricted to assigned tasks, and doors are kept closed except for put-away and retrieval.
8. Zone F holds the value-added services area. Inside Zone F, a fenced hazmat cage covers 60 m2 for segregated storage, alongside the designated areas for quarantine and rework.
9. Main transport aisles through the hall measure 4.0 m wide. Keep them free of pallets, waste and staged stock at all times to allow two-way truck movement.
10. Rack storage aisles between the high bays measure 3.0 m wide. Enter them only when authorised, observe priority signs, and never stage pallets inside the aisle profile.
11. Pedestrian routes cross the hall at defined points and connect all zones A-F. Use only those routes when moving on foot, remain clear of truck swept paths, and report any blocked or faded markings.
12. Memorise the zone sequence from goods-in to goods-out: Zone A for receiving at doors 1-4, Zone B for bulk storage, Zone C for picking, Zone D for dispatch at doors 5-8, Zone E for chilled storage, and Zone F for value-added services including the hazmat cage.

title: Shifts and supervision
text:
1. Harbourwick 3PL Ltd. operates the site on two staffed day shifts, Monday to Friday, under continuous supervision.
2. Shift 1 runs 06:00-14:00, Monday to Friday.
3. Shift 2 runs 14:00-22:00, Monday to Friday.
4. Outside those staffed hours the building remains closed unless overtime working has been expressly approved and supervised.

Accountability for the whole site rests in one place.
5. The warehouse manager is accountable for the whole site: operations, safety and final sign-offs.
6. During each shift that accountability is exercised on the floor through the designated shift leadership.
7. The shift supervisor runs one shift: floor staff and incident response.
8. Allocate one named shift supervisor to Shift 1 and one named shift supervisor to Shift 2.
9. Publish the names of the supervisors on duty where all floor staff can see them before work starts.
10. Direct all operational questions, task changes and safety concerns on a shift to the supervisor on duty for that shift.

Supervisors own the floor for their hours.
11. Start each shift with a brief face-to-face takeover between outgoing and incoming supervision.
12. Confirm staffing levels, open inbound and outbound work, equipment availability and any safety restrictions.
13. Keep floor staff within their assigned zones and tasks unless the shift supervisor reassigns them.
14. Respond immediately to any injury, damage, spill or equipment fault reported during the shift.
15. Record staffing changes, disruptions and open work for the next supervisor to continue without delay.
16. Escalate any matter beyond shift authority to the warehouse manager without waiting for the next working day.

Overtime control remains strictly centralised.
17. Only the warehouse manager may approve overtime.
18. Request overtime in advance with reason, numbers required and planned hours.
19. Do not start early, stay late or call in additional cover until approval has been given.
20. Assign a responsible supervisor to cover every approved overtime period.
21. Log approved overtime hours worked and retain the record for payroll and compliance review.

Continuity between Shift 1 and Shift 2 protects service and safety.
22. Overlap supervision long enough at 14:00 to transfer live information directly.
23. Hand over dock activity, work in progress, delayed loads and any personnel or equipment issues.
24. Ensure the incoming shift supervisor understands which tasks are complete, which remain open and which carry safety constraints.
25. Leave the floor, aisles and handover notes in a state the next shift can safely continue.

title: General floor rules and PPE
text:
1. Wear a high-visibility vest at all times on the warehouse floor. The requirement applies to everyone on the floor, including forklift operators, pickers, inbound operators, stock controllers, dispatchers, maintenance technicians, returns staff, shift supervisors, visitors and drivers under escort. Keep the vest fastened and visible over outer clothing. Replace soiled or faded vests through the shift supervisor.

2. Use safety footwear class S3 on the warehouse floor. Trainers, low shoes and open footwear are prohibited in all operational areas. Check soles, toecaps and fastenings before starting the shift. Report damaged footwear immediately and do not start floor work without compliant footwear.

3. As a forklift operator, fasten the seat belt whenever the truck is moving. Adjust the seat and belt before setting off. Keep the belt secured during travel, manoeuvring and ramp work. Stop the truck safely if the belt loosens or the retractor fails and report the defect for repair.

4. Apply PR-11 Pedestrian safety in the warehouse on every movement across the site. Use only segregated walkways and marked crossings. Give way to handling equipment at junctions and blind corners. Make eye contact with the driver before stepping in front of a truck. Never walk under raised forks or enter a working area closed by barriers.

5. Instruct all newcomers in PR-11 Pedestrian safety in the warehouse before they enter the floor unaccompanied. Show walkways, crossings, no-entry areas and waiting positions at the docks. Explain how to behave when a forklift approaches and where to stand during loading. Confirm understanding before assigning tasks.

6. Obey PR-14 Emergency evacuation without delay when the alarm sounds. Stop work, make equipment safe where it can be done instantly, and leave by the nearest safe exit route. Proceed directly to the assembly point. Remain there until the roll call is complete and the responsible supervisor authorises further action.

7. Keep fire exits, extinguishers, first-aid points and emergency signage clear and visible at all times. Do not block doors, hoses or alarm call points with pallets, waste or staging stock. Report missing or damaged signage to the shift supervisor on the same shift.

8. Maintain order on the floor throughout the shift. Remove strapping, film and spillages promptly. Park pallet jacks and handling aids in designated positions so aisles and exits remain passable. Store personal items only in assigned lockers and shelters, never on racking or beside machinery.

9. Report every hazard, near miss and injury to the shift supervisor without delay. Secure the area against further access where safe to do so. Do not attempt repairs to equipment, racking or electrical installations unless tasked and competent. Support the investigation by recording what was seen and preserving the scene as found.

title: Roles on the floor
text:
1. Warehouse manager provides site-wide leadership across all shifts and functions. Accountable for the whole site: operations, safety and final sign-offs. Authorises outcomes under PR-08 Stocktaking and cycle counts and PR-10 Forklift and MHE operation, retaining overtime decisions and major approvals.
2. Shift supervisor directs execution during assigned hours on the floor. Runs one shift: floor staff and incident response. Coordinating task allocation within the shift, responding first to incidents and escalating beyond-shift issues upward.
3. Forklift operators handle powered movement of unit loads between zones. Operates forklifts, reach trucks and pallet jacks. Working to PR-10 Forklift and MHE operation, holders move inbound pallets, feed replenishment and support loading without leaving equipment unattended.
4. Pickers complete customer order fulfilment at the pick face. Picks customer orders in Zone C against scanner tasks. Following PR-04 Order picking, sequence compliance, scan confirmation and location discipline remain core duties throughout the picking shift.
5. Inbound operators control the receiving end of the flow in Zone A. Unloads, counts and inspects inbound goods in Zone A. Assigned to PR-01 Inbound receiving, they verify documentation, unload vehicles, count cartons and record visible damage before system booking.
6. Stock controllers safeguard system accuracy for every location. Owns inventory accuracy: cycle counts, recounts and adjustments. Executing PR-08 Stocktaking and cycle counts on a rotating basis, investigators resolve discrepancies, request recounts and prepare adjustments for sign-off.
7. Returns staff manage reverse flow within Zone F. Inspects returns in Zone F and proposes restock, rework or scrap. Under PR-07 Returns handling, examiners grade condition, separate quarantine needs and recommend disposition for supervisory approval.
8. Maintenance technician preserves reliability of assets and infrastructure. Maintains MHE, racking and dock equipment and logs all repairs. Covering planned servicing, breakdown response and monthly racking checks, documentation of every intervention sustains audit traceability.
9. Dispatchers orchestrate outbound transport and door utilisation. Books transport, assigns dock doors and releases outbound loads. Operating PR-06 Outbound dispatch, planners book carriers, sequence staging and authorise loading only against released orders.

title: Approvals and ownership
text:
1. Stocktake results remain under single ownership. Only the warehouse manager may sign off stocktake results.

Under PR-08 Stocktaking and cycle counts, stock controllers prepare counts, recounts and adjustments for review. Submit the completed stocktake file for warehouse-manager sign-off before any final posting. Do not treat a shift-level check as final approval.

2. Damaged-goods write-offs follow a fixed monetary threshold. Damaged-goods write-offs above 750 EUR need warehouse-manager approval.

Apply the threshold to each write-off proposal separately under PR-09 Damaged-goods handling. Record the estimated value, cause and supporting inspection notes in the system. Route any case above 750 EUR to the warehouse manager without exception.

3. Lower-value write-offs stay with shift leadership. The shift supervisor approves damaged-goods write-offs up to 750 EUR.

Within that limit, the shift supervisor confirms quantity, value and disposal method. Forward the approved record to stock control for system adjustment. Escalate any doubtful valuation before approval.

4. Larger losses require senior sign-off. The warehouse manager approves damaged-goods write-offs above 750 EUR.

At this level the warehouse manager verifies evidence, decides on further investigation and authorises disposal or claim action. Retain the signed approval with the damaged-goods record in Zone F quarantine documentation. Do not scrap or release goods pending this decision.

5. Returns decisions have a separate owner. The shift supervisor approves the final disposition of inspected returns.

Under PR-07 Returns handling, returns staff inspect returns in Zone F and propose restock, rework or scrap. Present the inspection result and recommendation to the shift supervisor for decision. Implement restock, rework or scrap only after that approval.

6. Overtime cannot be authorised on the floor. Only the warehouse manager may approve overtime.

Request additional hours in advance with reason, affected shift and expected duration. Deploy overtime only after written warehouse-manager approval is received. Record approved hours for payroll and handover purposes.

7. Dock capacity is centrally controlled. The dispatcher assigns dock doors and time slots to carriers.

Coordinate with PR-01 Inbound receiving for inbound doors 1-4 and with PR-06 Outbound dispatch for outbound planning. Direct carriers to the assigned door and time only. Refer any clash or delay to the dispatcher for replanning.

8. Safety learning is owned on shift. The shift supervisor reviews every incident report.

Ensure each event on the floor is reported promptly with time, place, persons and equipment involved. Pass the report to the shift supervisor on the same shift for review. Carry out the corrective actions instructed after review and brief the next shift under PR-15 End-of-shift handover.

9. Access to powered trucks is restricted. Only the warehouse manager may authorise new forklift operators.

Under PR-10 Forklift and MHE operation, verify training, licence and practical assessment before nomination. Submit nominations to the warehouse manager for authorisation. Permit operation only after authorisation is granted and recorded.

title: Procedure system PR-01 to PR-15
text:
1. Apply PR-01 Inbound receiving for every inbound delivery without exception. Check transport documents at the dock, unload only after release, count and inspect the goods, and record any deviation immediately in the designated system.
2. Book every inspected pallet into stock before any physical movement under PR-02 Put-away to storage. Confirm the system-directed storage location on the scanner, transport the pallet directly there, and verify placement with a location scan.
3. Maintain full pick faces at the start of each picking shift through PR-03 Replenishment of pick faces. Monitor minimum levels continuously, pull reserve stock forward in time, and never allow picking to begin from an empty or unconfirmed location.
4. Pick strictly against scanner-directed tasks under PR-04 Order picking. Confirm each pick by scanning source and unit, place goods carefully into the order container, and report shortages or location errors without substituting stock.
5. Scan-verify all picked units before enclosing them as required by PR-05 Packing and labelling. Select the correct carton size, protect fragile items with approved materials, affix the system-generated label squarely, and release only complete orders.
6. Stage, check and load outbound work exclusively under PR-06 Outbound dispatch. Build loads by route and door plan, verify counts against dispatch documents, wrap and secure each pallet, and hand over sealed trailers with signed paperwork.
7. Process every customer return through PR-07 Returns handling inside the defined inspection area. Identify the order and reason, examine condition and completeness, segregate pending disposition, and post the system receipt without delay.
8. Sustain inventory accuracy every working day with PR-08 Stocktaking and cycle counts. Count the scheduled locations fully, investigate differences on the spot, perform the required recount before adjustment, and obtain authorised sign-off for results.
9. Isolate and document all non-conforming stock under PR-09 Damaged-goods handling. Move affected units to quarantine promptly, label the fault clearly, photograph where instructed, and await approved instructions for repair, downgrade or disposal.
10. Operate trucks, jacks and ancillary equipment only in line with PR-10 Forklift and MHE operation. Complete the documented pre-use check before first use, observe all site limits, park safely with power off, and report defects for immediate repair.
11. Protect people on foot at all times through PR-11 Pedestrian safety in the warehouse. Keep to marked walkways and crossings, wear required visibility and footwear protection, make eye contact with drivers, and never enter live traffic lanes.
12. Safeguard temperature-sensitive stock continuously with PR-12 Cold-chain handling. Transfer chilled goods quickly into the cold zone, keep doors closed, check temperature displays each entry, and escalate any excursion according to the response steps.
13. Control hazardous materials rigorously under PR-13 Hazmat handling and spill response. Store only approved quantities in the designated cage, follow segregation and labelling rules, use prescribed protective equipment, and execute spill containment immediately on release.
14. Evacuate calmly and completely whenever the alarm sounds under PR-14 Emergency evacuation. Stop all work, secure equipment if safe to do so, follow marked escape routes to the assembly point, and remain there until roll call authorises re-entry.
15. Transfer accountability cleanly between shifts with PR-15 End-of-shift handover. Summarise completed work, open orders and equipment status, highlight risks and pending carriers, and confirm the incoming supervisor accepts responsibility for the floor.

title: Carrier arrival and dock assignment
text:
1. Direct every inbound carrier to Zone A for receiving under PR-01 Inbound receiving.
2. Accept inbound trailers only at dock doors 1-4 reserved for receiving.
3. Hold all other doors for outbound movement and keep inbound vehicles clear of them.

Zone A is the receiving zone: inbound docks 1-4, unloading and goods inspection. Within Zone A coordinate unloading and goods inspection as one controlled flow from door to inspection area. Dispatchers book transport, assign dock doors and release outbound loads.

4. Obtain a confirmed time slot from the dispatcher before travelling to site.
5. Refuse entry to unscheduled arrivals until the dispatcher assigns a free inbound door and time slot.
6. Assign dock doors 1-4 and carrier time slots centrally through the dispatcher.

The building has 8 dock doors. Dock doors 1-4 serve inbound receiving. Because capacity at the receiving doors is limited, sequence arrivals strictly by the assigned slot order. Notify waiting drivers of delays promptly and reassign slots when an inbound door becomes available.

7. Book transport in advance so receiving labour and inspection capacity align with arrivals.
8. Assign each booked carrier a specific door from dock doors 1-4.
9. Release outbound loads separately and never promise an inbound carrier an outbound door.

The dispatcher assigns dock doors and time slots to carriers. Under that ownership, maintain a visible door plan for the current inbound queue. Record carrier name, registration, booked slot, actual arrival time and allocated door for every delivery. Instruct drivers to remain with the vehicle until called forward to the allocated door.

10. Call carriers forward one by one to the allocated inbound door.
11. Verify the door number on approach and stop only at the assigned dock.
12. Position the trailer squarely on the dock leveller before opening the rear doors.

Each of the 8 dock doors has a dock leveller. Confirm leveller availability as part of door assignment and report any fault immediately for maintenance action. Deploy inbound operators to the confirmed door only after the vehicle is braked, secured and the leveller is correctly seated. Begin document control and unloading in Zone A once docking is complete.

13. Close the inbound door after departure and update the door plan without delay.
14. Reallocate the vacated door to the next booked carrier in slot order.

title: Documents, unloading and inspection
text:
1. Verify the delivery note, purchase order reference and carrier identity at Zone A before opening the trailer under PR-01 Inbound receiving.
2. Reject mismatched or unannounced deliveries at inbound docks 1-4 without starting unloading under PR-01 Inbound receiving.
3. Position the trailer at the assigned dock in Zone A, the receiving zone for unloading and goods inspection, then apply brakes and wheel chocks.
4. Unload pallets and cartons by inbound operators in Zone A only after the document check passes under PR-01 Inbound receiving.
5. Count every pallet, carton and loose unit against the delivery note immediately on the dock apron.
6. Inspect packaging, labelling, quantities and visible damage before any system booking under PR-01 Inbound receiving.
7. Enter count and inspection results with the shared pool of 20 handheld WMS scanners used by pickers and inbound staff.
8. Transfer accepted goods to the marked inspection lanes in Zone A for measuring, weighing and label control.
9. Retain damaged, short-delivered or over-delivered goods separately and annotate the delivery note with quantities and defects.
10. Photograph visible transport damage and attach the images to the inbound record in the warehouse system.
11. Confirm temperature-sensitive or special-handling markings during inspection and route such goods to the applicable storage procedure.
12. Release only inspected and counted goods for system booking, since inspection precedes booking into the system under PR-01 Inbound receiving.
13. Notify the shift supervisor immediately of quantity variances, damage or missing documents and await instruction before proceeding.
14. Keep inbound operators responsible for unloading, counting and inspecting inbound goods in Zone A throughout the receiving operation.

title: Booking and release to put-away
text:
1. Finish inspection in Zone A before booking any inbound delivery into the warehouse system under PR-01 Inbound receiving.
2. Zone A is the receiving zone: inbound docks 1-4, unloading and goods inspection, and no receipt may be created while goods remain unchecked.
3. Inbound operators unload, count and inspect inbound goods in Zone A, recording quantity, damage and label discrepancies on the scanner.
4. Verify pallet quantity against the delivery note, check outer packaging for damage, and confirm product codes match the expected receipt.
5. Hold any damaged, short-delivered or unidentified goods at the inspection point and do not include them in the system booking quantity.
6. Book only inspected goods into the system, since inbound goods are inspected BEFORE they are booked into the system.
7. Create the system receipt immediately after inspection, entering the confirmed quantity, batch data where required, and the Zone A staging location.
8. Attach inspection results to the receipt so stock controllers can trace every booked pallet back to its count and condition.
9. Stock controllers own inventory accuracy: cycle counts, recounts and adjustments, and review each new receipt for plausibility before release.
10. Request correction of the receipt where the booked quantity differs from the inspection record, and do not release incorrect stock to put-away.
11. Release booked goods to put-away only under PR-02 Put-away to storage, using the system-directed destination for Zone B, Zone C, Zone E or Zone F.
12. Observe the fixed sequence that goods are booked into the system BEFORE put-away to storage, and never move pallets to racking on an unbooked instruction.
13. Print or activate pallet labels at booking and ensure each pallet carries its identifier before leaving Zone A.
14. Stage released pallets by destination to keep forklift collection orderly, and hand the system move tasks to the put-away team without delay.
15. Close the PR-01 Inbound receiving task in the system once booking and release are complete, leaving only held quantities open for resolution.

title: Bulk storage in Zone B
text:
1. Operate Zone B strictly as the bulk storage zone with high-bay pallet racking under PR-02 Put-away to storage.
2. Store all reserve and bulk stock inside the high-bay racking, which provides 2,400 pallet positions.
3. Place only one pallet identifier per rack position and confirm the booking with the WMS scanner before leaving the bay.
4. Respect the structural limit of each rack bay at all times; each rack bay may carry at most 2,700 kg.
5. Verify pallet weight before lifting to the beams, because a pallet, including its load, may weigh at most 900 kg.
6. Split any consignment that would overload a single bay across two or more bays in the same aisle.
7. Use only the assigned reach trucks for all high-bay movements; the fleet provides 5 reach trucks for the high bays.
8. Observe the rated capacity of the reach trucks at 2.0 t and never attempt to lift heavier unit loads with them.
9. Assign Forklift operators trained on reach trucks to Zone B put-away and retrieval tasks.
10. Keep Stock controllers responsible for monitoring bay utilisation and reporting overloads or damage immediately.
11. Maintain main transport aisles through Zone B at 4.0 m wide and keep them completely clear of staged pallets, wrapping material and handling equipment.
12. Maintain rack storage aisles at 3.0 m wide and prohibit parking or double-staging inside them during put-away.
13. Drive at walking pace when entering a storage aisle and yield to a reach truck already positioned at a bay face.
14. Apply free block stacking only in marked floor areas outside the racking and never inside the storage aisles.
15. Limit any free block stack to 3 pallets high.
16. Limit any free block stack to 3.5 m in height, even where three low pallets would remain below that height.
17. Check stack stability, pallet quality and load overhang before adding the second or third pallet.
18. Report leaning stacks, broken boards or shifted loads to the shift supervisor and do not add further pallets to an unstable stack.
19. Return damaged pallets to the designated area and re-palletise the goods before returning them to Zone B.
20. Complete every put-away under PR-02 Put-away to storage by scanning the final bay location so inventory accuracy remains intact for replenishment and picking.

Zone B feeds the ground-level pick faces in the adjacent zone. Accurate bay discipline here prevents shortages, double handling and unsafe overloads downstream.

Coordinate with maintenance staff when rack impact, bent beams or missing safety pins are found. Isolate the affected bay until it has been inspected and released back to use.

title: Put-away process
text:
1. Execute PR-02 Put-away to storage for every pallet released from receiving and move only system-booked goods to their storage destination.

2. Confirm in the WMS that inbound goods were inspected before booking, because inspection always precedes system booking, and never start put-away when the booking receipt is missing or incomplete.

3. Release pallets to put-away strictly after system booking, since goods are booked into the system before put-away to storage, and return any unbooked pallet to receiving for completion of the inbound steps.

4. Assign Forklift operators to all put-away transport, as Forklift operators operate forklifts, reach trucks and pallet jacks, and select the truck type that suits the pallet weight, height and destination aisle.

5. Direct ambient bulk pallets to Zone B, noting that Zone B is the bulk storage zone: high-bay pallet racking, and follow the WMS location instruction for aisle, bay and level without substituting an alternative position.

6. Transport chilled pallets immediately to Zone E, noting that Zone E is the cold zone: chilled storage held at +2 to +6 °C, and minimise door-open and staging time to protect the temperature range.

7. Deliver pallets requiring labelling, kitting, inspection or other special treatment to Zone F, noting that Zone F holds the value-added services area, and hand over each pallet to the responsible staff at the defined drop point.

8. Scan every put-away at the destination location and verify that the WMS confirms the correct zone and position for Zone B, Zone E or Zone F.

9. Report missing labels, unreadable barcodes, damaged pallets or occupied locations immediately and leave the pallet in a safe holding position until the system instruction is corrected.

10. Close PR-02 Put-away to storage in the WMS only after all pallets from the booking have a confirmed storage location, thereby keeping booked stock, physical location and system inventory fully aligned for replenishment and picking.

11. Keep put-away lanes and staging areas clear during the operation and return handling equipment to its parking position once the last pallet of the booking is stored.

title: Cold storage in Zone E
text:
1. Hold all chilled stock only in Zone E in line with PR-12 Cold-chain handling.
2. Maintain Zone E within its chilled range at all times during storage and put-away.
3. Verify the cold-zone temperature manually each shift and record the reading.
4. Prioritise cold-chain pallets at put-away and minimise time outside Zone E.
5. Segregate non-conforming chilled stock immediately and escalate under PR-12 Cold-chain handling.

Zone E is the cold zone: chilled storage held at +2 to +6 °C. Do not use Zone E for ambient, quarantine or general bulk overflow. Keep the boundary to the rest of the warehouse closed except for direct put-away, replenishment and collection moves.

6. Keep the cold zone at or above +2 °C. Treat any reading below +2 °C as a breach.
7. Keep the cold zone at or below +6 °C. Treat any reading above +6 °C as a breach.
8. Check the fixed display on entry and confirm it with the manual verification for the shift.
9. Log each shift verification with time and initials in the designated record.
10. Re-verify after any prolonged door opening, defrost cycle or maintenance work.

Manual verification each shift is mandatory and does not replace continuous monitoring where fitted. Never rely on memory or on the previous shift reading. Record the actual observed value at the time of the check and sign for it.

11. Move chilled inbound pallets to Zone E without delay after release from receiving.
12. Transport chilled goods in closed load units and do not stage them in ambient aisles.
13. Rotate chilled stock by expiry date and keep labels visible for scanner tasks.
14. Leave air circulation gaps around pallets and do not block coolers or sensors.
15. Keep Zone E floors dry, clear of packaging waste and free of ice build-up.

Apply PR-12 Cold-chain handling to every receipt, put-away, replenishment, pick and return that touches chilled product. Follow its steps for temperature evidence, time limits outside the chamber and handling of insulated containers. Where PR-12 Cold-chain handling requires a hold, place the stock on hold and prevent further picking until release.

16. Stop normal put-away into Zone E on any temperature breach and contain stock already inside.
17. Quarantine product exposed to out-of-range conditions pending a documented decision.
18. Report every breach, probe failure and missing shift check without delay for review.
19. Do not release breached chilled stock to picking, packing or dispatch without authorisation.
20. Restore the +2 to +6 °C range and prove stability with a fresh verification before resuming normal moves.

Discipline in Zone E protects product safety and stock accuracy. Maintain the +2 to +6 °C envelope, verify it manually each shift, work strictly to PR-12 Cold-chain handling, and keep full records to show the cold chain was never broken.

title: Hazmat cage and quarantine in Zone F
text:
1. Treat Zone F as the controlled area for all restricted and undecided stock, because Zone F holds the value-added services area and provides the physical separation required for Storage and Put-Away.
2. Keep the hazmat cage locked, signed and accessible only to instructed staff, since the hazmat cage is inside Zone F and must remain isolated from general bulk and picking flows.
3. Store all classified hazardous goods only inside the fenced cage, which inside Zone F covers 60 m2, and never place hazmat pallets in open floor areas, aisles or alongside general stock.
4. Limit the total quantity in the cage at all times, as no more than 3,000 kg of hazmat may be stored in the hazmat cage at one time, and check the stock total before every additional put-away.
5. Check hazmat cage stock weight before every put-away and reject any receipt exceeding 3000 kg, rather than overfilling the cage or stacking outside its fence.
6. Follow PR-13 Hazmat handling and spill response for every receipt, put-away, pick and spill in the cage, including segregation, labelling, containment and immediate clean-up actions.
7. Reserve the marked quarantine holding inside Zone F for suspect, damaged or unreleased product, because the quarantine area is in Zone F and provides system-blocked separation from available inventory.
8. Move goods to quarantine immediately when documents, labels, condition or system status are unclear, and release them only after inspection, approval and system clearance.
9. Inspect all customer returns in the designated inspection bays, since returns are inspected in Zone F, and keep them apart from new inbound goods and from the hazmat cage.
10. Handle damaged units found during storage or returns inspection under PR-09 Damaged-goods handling, transferring them to quarantine, recording the damage, and awaiting a decision on restock, rework or scrap.
11. Maintain clear walkways, separation distances and fire access around the cage and quarantine pens at all times, and return spill kits, barriers and inspection tools to their marked positions after use.
12. Record every cage and quarantine movement in the warehouse system on completion, confirming location, quantity and hazard status, so put-away records remain accurate and restricted stock cannot be allocated to normal orders.

title: Picking zone layout
text:
1. Zone C is the picking zone: ground-level pick faces and flow racks.
2. Hold all forward stock for customer orders only on those ground-level faces and flow racks. Reserve upper levels and bulk holdings outside Zone C for replenishment supply.
3. Lay out each pick face with a single SKU facing the operator aisle. Keep labels, barcodes and location identifiers forward-facing and scannable at all times.
4. Use flow racks for small-quantity, high-rotation lines. Load flow lanes from the rear replenishment side and pick from the front operator side to enforce first-in first-out rotation.
5. Pickers pick customer orders in Zone C against scanner tasks. Accept no paper lists, verbal instructions or retyped picks inside the zone.
6. Execute every pick under PR-04 Order picking. Confirm each unit by scanning the location label and then the unit label before placing goods into the order container.
7. Pickers and inbound staff share 20 handheld WMS scanners. Sign a device out at the start of work in Zone C and return it to charge at the end of work.
8. Report a faulty or unreadable scanner immediately and exchange it for a serviceable unit. Never continue picking in Zone C without an active scanner session.
9. Feed all pick faces from bulk under PR-03 Replenishment of pick faces. Trigger replenishment when the WMS signals low forward quantity and block picking from a face flagged empty.
10. Keep replenishment movement and order picking separated within the face. Pause picking at a lane while replenishment is loading from the rear and resume only after the lane is released.
11. Maintain clear segregation between forward pick stock and packed orders awaiting transfer. Move completed order containers promptly out of the pick face to the designated transfer point.
12. Keep the operator aisle in front of every pick face free of pallets, wrapping material and empty cartons. Stage empty pallets and waste only at the marked collection points.
13. Apply FIFO discipline across all flow racks and ground-level faces. Place newly replenished stock behind existing forward stock and never cover expiry or batch markings.
14. Inspect pick faces during routine patrols for damaged packaging, loose cartons or overhanging goods. Restack lightly displaced cartons immediately and escalate any unsafe face for replenishment correction.
15. Close a pick face in the system when the SKU changes or the face is damaged. Open a new face only after the location, label and system record match exactly.
16. Return unused units to their correct pick face at once when an order is cancelled or short-picked. Scan the return to the location and never leave surplus stock on the floor or on top of racks.
17. Sustain readiness of Zone C for the next replenishment cycle by clearing debris, aligning containers and verifying that every face shows a readable label before handover.

title: Replenishment of pick faces
text:
1. Execute PR-03 Replenishment of pick faces as the first warehouse task of the day. Pick faces are replenished BEFORE the picking shift starts, and no order picking begins on an unfilled face.

2. Draw all replenishment stock from bulk reserve. Zone B is the bulk storage zone: high-bay pallet racking. Collect only released pallets booked to the system and staged for transfer.

3. Deliver replenishment only to its assigned face in the picking area. Zone C is the picking zone: ground-level pick faces and flow racks. Place cartons forward-facing, labels outward, and keep each SKU strictly on its designated face.

4. Direct forklift operators to bring down full pallets and cartons for the faces. Instruct pickers to remain clear of the faces while replenishment trucks are working in the aisle. Require inbound operators to finish any late put-away so reserve pallets are accessible.

5. Task stock controllers with triggering replenishment from inventory accuracy data. Confirm the WMS replenishment task on the handheld scanner before moving stock. Scan the bulk pallet, scan the destination pick face, and book every quantity moved.

6. Keep flow racks filled from the rear and never top up from the picking side. Push existing cartons forward, load new cartons behind them, and verify that rollers run freely. Remove crushed cartons or broken packaging immediately.

7. Maintain clear separation during replenishment work. Obey segregated walkways, keep handling equipment clear of pickers, and stack empty pallets neatly for removal. Stop work and secure the load if cartons lean, slip, or block the operator aisle.

8. Report shortages, damage, or misplaced reserve pallets to the shift supervisor without delay. The shift supervisor runs one shift: floor staff and incident response. Do not substitute another SKU or overfill a face to hide a shortfall.

9. Close PR-03 Replenishment of pick faces only when every scheduled face is filled, scanned, and ready. Hand the completed replenishment tasks to the picking team. Release Zone C for order picking only after replenishment is confirmed complete.

title: Order picking with scanners
text:
1. Execute PR-04 Order picking only in Zone C against WMS scanner tasks.
Zone C is the picking zone: ground-level pick faces and flow racks.
Do not pick from reserve storage, staged inbound goods, or any other zone.

2. Confirm replenishment is complete before starting the picking shift.
Pick faces are replenished BEFORE the picking shift starts under PR-03 Replenishment of pick faces.
Check the scanner queue for replenishment holds or shortages before taking the first task.

3. Draw a handheld WMS scanner at shift start and log on with your personal user ID.
Pickers and inbound staff share 20 handheld WMS scanners.
Return damaged units, units with low battery, or units with unreadable displays to the charging station immediately and request a replacement.

4. Follow the task sequence shown on the scanner display without deviation.
Pickers pick customer orders in Zone C against scanner tasks.
Travel to the directed pick face location, verify the location code on the rack label, and confirm arrival only when you stand at the correct face.

5. Pick the displayed SKU in the displayed quantity into the directed order container.
Handle each unit by its outer packaging and keep labels visible for the next scan.
Place heavy units at the bottom of the container and keep fragile units on top.

6. Scan-verify every picked unit at the pick face before leaving the location.
Picked items are scan-verified BEFORE packing under PR-04 Order picking and PR-05 Packing and labelling.
If the scanner rejects the unit barcode, stop and compare SKU, batch, and expiry against the task.

7. Report mismatches, damaged stock, empty faces, or unreadable labels from the scanner menu without delay.
Leave the container at the face, retain the task on your scanner, and wait for correction instructions.
Never substitute a similar SKU, take stock from an adjacent face, or force-confirm a failed scan.

8. Complete the task on the scanner only after all lines show verified status.
Close the order container, attach the task label where required, and move the container to the designated transfer point for packing.
Keep the transfer point clear and never obstruct the operator aisle or collection points.

9. Release the scanner task and accept the next task in queue order.
Do not carry two open order containers, split one task across two pickers, or interleave tasks unless the scanner explicitly directs a multi-order run.
Maintain custody of the container until handover to packing.

10. Hand over verified containers and the scanner at shift end according to the handover instruction.
Log off the scanner, place it in the charger, and report incomplete tasks, repeated scan failures, and faces needing replenishment to the responsible supervisor.
Do not leave unverified containers in Zone C for the next shift.

title: Packing and labelling
text:
1. Execute PR-05 Packing and labelling for every order container transferred from PR-04 Order picking before release to PR-06 Outbound dispatch.
2. Accept only complete order containers at the packing benches. Pickers pick customer orders in Zone C against scanner tasks and forward closed containers with intact labels.
3. Scan-verify each picked item BEFORE packing. Hold the container at the bench until the system confirms quantity and identity for every line.
4. Quarantine any container with a scan mismatch, short quantity, damaged unit or unreadable label. Do not pack disputed items into the outbound carton or onto the outbound pallet.
5. Select the correct carton size and cushioning for the verified goods. Place heavier items at the bottom and fill voids to prevent movement during transport.
6. Seal cartons squarely with tape along the centre seam and both edges. Affix the shipping label flat on the largest face where scanners and drivers can read it without turning the carton.
7. Build outbound pallets by order and route in packing sequence. Stack cartons interlocked, labels outward, within the pallet footprint without overhang.
8. Transfer each built pallet to Dispatch uses 2 semi-automatic stretch wrappers. Wrap every outbound pallet to base-to-top stability before staging.
9. Operate the stretch wrappers only with trained hands clear of the turntable. Cut and secure the film tail on every pallet and check corners for tearing or loose wraps.
10. Feed all empty cartons, dividers and paper void-fill to the site has 1 cardboard baler. Bale cardboard continuously during packing to keep benches and aisles clear.
11. Keep baler feed free of stretch film, strapping, labels and general waste. Stop the baler immediately on jam or unusual noise and call for qualified clearance.
12. Stage finished, wrapped and labelled pallets for collection to Zone D is the dispatch zone: outbound staging in front of docks 5-8. Hand the load information to Dispatchers book transport, assign dock doors and release outbound loads for onward movement under PR-06 Outbound dispatch.

title: Dispatch staging in Zone D
text:
1. Stage every wrapped and labelled pallet in Zone D before loading under PR-06 Outbound dispatch.
2. Confirm each container has completed PR-05 Packing and labelling before transfer to staging.
3. Zone D is the dispatch zone: outbound staging in front of docks 5-8.
4. The building has 8 dock doors.
5. Dock doors 5-8 serve outbound dispatch.
6. There are 4 outbound dock doors.
7. Each of the 8 dock doors has a dock leveller.
8. Dispatch uses 2 semi-automatic stretch wrappers.
9. Direct wrapped pallets from packing to the assigned staging lane without delay.
10. Position pallets squarely inside the marked staging bays facing the assigned door.
11. Group each load together by door, route and loading sequence.
12. Leave access gaps between loads for inspection and forklift manoeuvring.
13. Operate the stretch wrappers in turn to avoid queues from packing.
14. Inspect film tension and edge coverage immediately after wrapping.
15. Rewrap any pallet showing loose film, exposed corners or unstable layers.
16. Allocate staging space strictly within Zone D and never beyond the marked boundaries.
17. Align pallet labels outward so identifiers remain visible from the aisle.
18. Secure staged pallets against movement while awaiting collection.
19. Verify door assignment on the staging board before placing pallets down.
20. Coordinate door changes promptly when dispatch instructions are updated.
21. Keep the approach to every dock leveller completely clear of pallets and waste.
22. Check leveller plates are seated and dock doors fully open before loading starts.
23. Report faulty levellers, damaged doors or blocked staging lanes for repair immediately.
24. Release only complete, documented loads from staging to the loading team.
25. Maintain continuous flow from staging lanes through the assigned door onto the trailer.
26. Separate urgent or partial loads in the designated overflow bay without mixing other loads.
27. Document every staged pallet movement accurately to preserve load traceability.

title: Load release and truck loading
text:
1. Execute PR-06 Outbound dispatch only in Zone D for every trailer departure. Stage sealed and labelled pallets in Zone D is the dispatch zone: outbound staging in front of docks 5-8, sorted by load and departure sequence. Release no vehicle until packing, labelling and wrapping checks are confirmed complete in the system.

2. Assign the loading door through the dispatcher. Dock doors 5-8 serve outbound dispatch, and no other door shall be used for outbound loading without reassignment. Confirm the door allocation on the departure board before moving pallets to the leveller.

3. Book transport in advance and lock the time slot to the assigned door. Dispatchers book transport, assign dock doors and release outbound loads. Verify carrier identity, registration number and booked reference at the gate, then direct the driver to the allocated door in Zone D.

4. Direct dock positioning and supervise reversing to the leveller. The dispatcher assigns dock doors and time slots to carriers. Instruct the driver to stop, apply brakes and hand over keys where required by local instruction. Place the dock restraint or wheel chock before opening the trailer doors.

5. Check trailer condition before loading starts. Inspect floor integrity, side curtains, roof, lights and cleanliness for general cargo suitability. Reject contaminated, damaged or unsafe trailers and notify the dispatcher immediately for replacement booking.

6. Load pallets strictly in the dispatcher release sequence. Place heavy pallets at the front over the axles and lighter pallets toward the rear using generic load distribution guidance. Secure every row against shifting with appropriate restraints. Count each pallet onto the trailer and confirm the running total against the load list.

7. Reconcile the loaded quantity with the release documentation before closing the doors. Resolve any shortfall or surplus while the trailer remains at the door. Obtain dispatcher release authorisation for the final load, attach the delivery notes and record the seal number against the departure.

8. Seal the trailer and release the vehicle from Zone D. Close and lock both doors, fit the numbered seal and photograph the sealed closure for the file where required. Hand the signed documents to the driver, log departure time in the dispatch record and clear the staging area in front of docks 5-8 for the next PR-06 Outbound dispatch load.

title: Pallet weight and trailer capacity
text:
1. Apply a single maximum pallet weight to every outbound load plan. A pallet, including its load, may weigh at most 900 kg. Use this figure as the planning weight for stability checks, weight totals and transport bookings, even when the actual pallet weighs less.

Assess each order against that limit before wrapping and staging. Reject overweight pallets for rework into compliant units. Record the verified weight in the release documentation covered under PR-06 Outbound dispatch.

2. Plan curtain-side trailer loads against payload first. Our contracted curtain-side trailers carry a payload of 26000 kg. Divide that payload by the maximum pallet weight to establish the weight-constrained limit.

Calculate 26000 kg divided by 900 kg per pallet to give 28 pallets. Treat this quotient as a hard ceiling for full-weight pallets. Do not round upward or add an additional pallet on the assumption of lighter average weight without a documented re-weigh.

3. Compare the weight result with the physical floor capacity. A trailer has 33 floor pallet positions. Position count sets the volume footprint available for standard pallets placed on the trailer bed.

Count positions from the headboard to the rear doors without double-stacking unless the load plan expressly permits it. Leave damaged floor sections empty and reduce the usable count accordingly.

4. Govern every full-weight movement by the lower of the two limits. A trailer takes at most 28 full-weight pallets (payload divided by maximum pallet weight, capped by floor positions).

Explain the outcome to loading teams in plain terms. Weight restricts the load before space does. Five floor positions remain theoretically vacant when carrying 28 pallets at 900 kg each, because adding a 29th full-weight pallet would exceed the 26000 kg payload.

5. Build mixed-weight loads within the same ceiling. Sum the actual verified weights of all pallets on the consignment. Keep the total at or below 26000 kg and the pallet count at or below 33 floor pallet positions.

Allocate heavier pallets over the axles and distribute weight evenly along the bed. Secure each row to prevent shifting during transit. Reconcile the final loaded quantity and weight against the release paperwork before closing the doors.

6. Document exceptions and partial loads consistently. Where pallets weigh less than 900 kg, more than 28 physical pallets may travel provided neither the 26000 kg payload nor the 33 floor pallet positions are exceeded.

Enter the per-pallet weights, total weight and position count on the load sheet. Retain the calculation for audit and driver handover. Escalate any request to exceed either limit through the normal dispatch control before loading.

7. Enforce the limit at staging and loading. Check pallet weights at wrapping, verify totals at staging, and re-confirm before truck departure. Refuse to load a 29th full-weight pallet onto a trailer already carrying 28 pallets at maximum weight, even where empty floor space remains visible.

title: Van and shift dispatch limit
text:
1. Use the delivery van only for small consignments that cannot justify a trailer movement. Our delivery van carries a payload of 1800 kg.
2. Plan van loading against floor space as well as weight. The delivery van has 6 pallet positions.
3. Apply the full-weight limit as the binding constraint for heavy pallets. The van takes at most 2 full-weight pallets; heavier orders go by trailer.
4. Assign any order exceeding the van limit to trailer transport under PR-06 Outbound dispatch. Do not split a heavy pallet across van positions to circumvent the weight limit.
5. Stage van consignments in Zone D separately from trailer staging. Zone D is the dispatch zone: outbound staging in front of docks 5-8.
6. Release van departures through the same dispatch control as trailers. The dispatcher assigns dock doors and time slots to carriers.
7. Treat the van as overflow and urban-drop capacity, not as part of the per-shift pallet promise. Record van pallets separately from trailer load counts in the release documentation.
8. Plan trailer throughput from fixed door capacity. There are 4 outbound dock doors.
9. Dock doors 5-8 serve outbound dispatch. No inbound receiving may occupy these doors during scheduled outbound loading.
10. Schedule loading to the standard turnaround. Each outbound door handles 4 trailer loads per shift.
11. Calculate the shift promise from doors multiplied by loads per shift. Outbound capacity is at most 448 full-weight pallets per shift (doors x loads per shift x pallets per trailer).
12. Commit to customers only within that ceiling. Accept additional bookings for the same shift only when a booked load cancels and the dispatcher releases the door slot.
13. Sequence staging, wrapping checks and reconciliation so each door completes its 4 loads without queuing into the next shift. Hold late-arriving trailers for the following shift rather than overloading doors, labour or yard space.
14. Coordinate van movements so they do not block trailer access to docks 5-8. Load the van from the marked staging area and dispatch it between trailer manoeuvres.
15. Report any door taken out of service, trailer rejection or labour shortfall to the dispatcher immediately. Reduce the promised pallet quantity for that shift pro rata and rebook the balance.

title: Hazmat cage pallet limit
text:
1. Store no more than 3,000 kg of hazmat in the hazmat cage at one time.
2. Treat the 3,000 kg limit as absolute for all classified stock combined, regardless of packaging type or dwell time.
3. Apply a maximum gross weight of 900 kg to every pallet, including its load, before assessing cage capacity.
4. Derive cage pallet capacity by dividing the hazmat stock limit by the maximum pallet weight.
5. Hold at most 3 full-weight pallets in the hazmat cage at any moment.

Locate the hazmat cage inside Zone F. Operate all receipts, storage and issues under PR-13 Hazmat handling and spill response. Confine the fenced installation to its defined footprint of 60 m2.

6. Plan inbound put-away against remaining weight allowance rather than visible floor space.
7. Weigh any doubtful pallet on calibrated equipment before admission to the cage.
8. Reject admission when the next pallet would push total cage content above 3,000 kg.
9. Stage the excess quantity outside the cage in approved holding only until weight allowance becomes available.
10. Record every movement in and out by weight so the live total remains visible.
11. Reduce pallet count below 3 where individual pallets approach 900 kg and combined weight nears the ceiling.
12. Permit more than 3 physical pallets only where documented lighter weights keep the combined total at or below 3,000 kg.
13. Count mixed full-weight and part-weight loads together toward the same limit.
14. Never use the 60 m2 floor area as justification for exceeding the weight ceiling.

Inside Zone F, segregation remains mandatory even when the cage holds fewer than 3 full-weight pallets. Maintain separation from incompatible classes, keep aisles clear for inspection, and preserve access to spill equipment at all times.

15. Check cage total before accepting a transfer from receiving, replenishment or returns.
16. Withdraw or consume existing stock first when an incoming hazmat delivery would otherwise breach the limit.
17. Escalate immediately where committed orders and on-hand stock together exceed available allowance.
18. Document weight calculations on the stock record to show division of the hazmat stock limit by the maximum pallet weight.
19. Audit the cage total at each transaction and correct discrepancies before further put-away.
20. Enforce the 3 full-weight pallet rule during shift changes, overtime working and peak inbound periods without exception.

title: Daily cycle counts
text:
1. Execute all work in this section under PR-08 Stocktaking and cycle counts.
2. Stock controllers own inventory accuracy: cycle counts, recounts and adjustments.
3. Run cycle counts every working day on a rotating zone schedule.
4. Plan the rotation so each storage area returns into scope at its defined interval.
5. Publish the daily count scope before the shift starts.
6. Assign count tasks by location, not by expected quantity.
7. Count from the physical stock first, then compare with the system figure.
8. Record every count directly in the WMS scanner at the location.
9. Keep pallets and cartons in place until the count for that location is finished.
10. Pause put-away, replenishment and picking moves for locations under active count.
11. Resume moves for a location only after the counter releases it.
12. Reconcile the first count against the system balance immediately.
13. Order a recount for every location with a variance.
14. Assign the recount to a different counter where staffing allows.
15. Perform a second count BEFORE any stock adjustment is posted.
16. Post no adjustment on a first-count difference alone.
17. Investigate the cause when the second count confirms a discrepancy.
18. Check recent receipts, put-away bookings, picks, replenishments and returns for the SKU.
19. Verify unit of measure errors, transposed digits and misplaced pallets before adjusting.
20. Correct a misplaced pallet by moving and scanning it to the right location.
21. Post the system adjustment only from the confirmed recount result.
22. Document the reason code for every adjustment in the system.
23. Escalate repeated variances for the same location or SKU to further review.
24. Track daily completion of the rotating zone schedule to completion.
25. Carry forward no unfinished count locations without explicit handover.
26. Hand over open counts, recounts and pending adjustments at PR-15 End-of-shift handover.
27. Stock controllers review the daily results for accuracy trends and follow-up actions.
28. Within PR-08 Stocktaking and cycle counts, discipline depends on sequencing.
29. Daily coverage builds accuracy progressively through the rotating zone schedule.
30. Ownership stays clear because stock controllers own inventory accuracy: cycle counts, recounts and adjustments.
31. Integrity stays protected because a second count happens BEFORE any stock adjustment is posted.
32. Apply this discipline every working day, since cycle counts run every working day on a rotating zone schedule.
33. Close each day with counted locations reconciled, recounted where needed, and adjusted only on verified results.

title: Annual wall-to-wall stocktake
text:
1. Execute PR-08 Stocktaking and cycle counts as a full wall-to-wall stocktake once a year across all storage locations.
2. Freeze all inbound, outbound, replenishment and internal moves for the stocktake window before counting starts.
3. Assign counting teams by zone and aisle so every pallet position, pick face, bulk floor area and controlled store is counted once and only once.
4. Place stock controllers in charge of inventory accuracy for the event: cycle counts, recounts and adjustments.
5. Brief all counters on scan discipline, label handling, damage reporting and escalation before releasing them to the floor.
6. Count every location from physical stock and record the physical quantity without viewing the system figure during the first pass.
7. Compare each first count with the system quantity immediately after it is entered and flag every variance for follow-up.
8. Order a second count for each location with a variance before any stock adjustment is posted.
9. Allocate recounts to counters who did not perform the first count in that location.
10. Investigate persistent differences through document checks, adjacent-location checks, quarantine checks and recent movement history before proposing an adjustment.
11. Submit all proposed adjustments with first-count evidence, recount evidence and variance explanation to the warehouse manager for review.
12. Obtain sign-off of the stocktake results only from the warehouse manager.
13. Post approved adjustments to the system only after that sign-off has been recorded.
14. Reconcile the full site balance after posting and confirm zero uncounted locations, zero open recounts and zero unsigned adjustments remain.
15. Archive count sheets, recount records, adjustment logs and the signed result as the audit trail for PR-08 Stocktaking and cycle counts.

The warehouse manager remains accountable for the whole site: operations, safety and final sign-offs, and therefore retains final authority over shutdown timing, staffing, move freeze and release back to operation. Stock controllers own preparation of count maps, sequencing of zones, control of recounts and preparation of the adjustment proposal pack. No other role may close the event, approve the final balance or authorise posting of wall-to-wall adjustments.

Release the site back to normal work only after the warehouse manager has signed off the stocktake results and confirmed that all adjustments are posted. Communicate completion, system availability and any corrected location rules to the next operational team without delay.

title: Racking care and stock accuracy
text:
1. Keep all bulk pallet stock inside the high-bay racking. Zone B is the bulk storage zone: high-bay pallet racking. Place no reserve pallet outside its assigned rack position except under PR-02 Put-away to storage or PR-03 Replenishment of pick faces. Report any pallet found outside address immediately for rebooking.

The high-bay racking provides 2,400 pallet positions. Treat every position as a controlled inventory address. Book each put-away, replenishment removal, and relocation by scanner without delay. Leave no pallet physically moved without a matching system movement.

2. Respect the structural limit of every bay. Each rack bay may carry at most 2,700 kg. Calculate the bay total from all levels before adding another pallet. Split heavy consignments across adjacent bays rather than concentrating weight in one bay.

Check label weights during PR-02 Put-away to storage and during PR-08 Stocktaking and cycle counts. Stop put-away to any bay showing deformation, cracking, or loose fixings. Barricade the affected bay and notify supervision before continuing work in the aisle.

3. Protect uprights, beams, and bracing from impact. Approach bays squarely and lift clear of beams before reversing. Lower pallets centrally onto both support beams. Remove any twisted, broken-board, or overhanging pallet from racking and transfer it for rework.

Never climb racking, store goods directly on bracing, or place loose cartons into a pallet position. Keep rack storage aisles free of empty pallets, stretch film, and debris after each task. Return handling equipment to its parking area when the task ends.

4. Maintain the monthly inspection regime without exception. Racking gets a documented safety inspection every month. Support the inspection by clearing beam levels for visual access and by reporting earlier damage without waiting for the due date.

The maintenance technician maintains MHE, racking and dock equipment and logs all repairs. Direct all beam damage, missing safety pins, anchor defects, and levelling faults to that route. Prohibit use of any bay marked out of service until the repair log confirms release.

5. Keep rack stock equal to the system at all times. Count from physical stock first under PR-08 Stocktaking and cycle counts, then compare with the system figure. Investigate overages as carefully as shortages, including wrong bay, wrong level, and duplicated labels.

Reconfirm any adjusted location by a second physical check before closing the task. Escalate repeated variances at the same address for bay audit, scanner review, and process correction. Release frozen moves only through the authorised procedure.

6. Control housekeeping around the racking footprint. Verify beam signage, bay numbering, and weight notices remain legible. Replace damaged labels through the stock control route rather than handwriting over them. Record every inspection, damage report, repair, and adjustment so the history of each bay remains traceable.

title: Returns acceptance and inspection
text:
1. Execute all returns work under PR-07 Returns handling from receipt to inspection record.
2. Zone F holds the value-added services area and provides the controlled space for returns receipt, opening, checking and segregation.
3. Accept returns only within 14 days of delivery and reject any consignment outside that window under PR-07 Returns handling.
4. Direct the carrier or driver to the designated returns point and obtain the delivery note, return authorisation and reason for return before unloading.
5. Verify the returned quantity against the authorisation line by line and record shortages, overages or substitution immediately in the returns log.
6. Returns are inspected in Zone F and no inspection may take place in receiving, bulk, picking or dispatch areas.
7. Transfer every carton or unit to the Zone F inspection benches without delay and keep returns physically separate from new inbound stock and outbound orders.
8. Returns staff inspect returns in Zone F and propose restock, rework or scrap for each inspected line.
9. Open each returned package, check the item identity, quantity, condition, labelling, seals and expiry or batch marking where applicable.
10. Photograph visible damage, contamination, tampering or incorrect items and attach the images to the inspection record for traceability.
11. Grade each unit as suitable for restock, requiring rework, or requiring scrap, and place it in the corresponding marked location pending a formal disposition decision.
12. Returns are inspected BEFORE any restock, rework or scrap decision and do not move inspected goods to storage, rework or disposal until that decision is issued.
13. Complete the PR-07 Returns handling inspection record for every return, including date of original delivery, date of receipt, SKU, quantity received, quantity inspected and proposed disposition.
14. Escalate suspected cold-chain breach, hazardous leakage, pest evidence or counterfeit marking to the responsible supervisor before further handling.
15. Keep the Zone F returns area clear, swept and free of packaging waste at the end of each inspection, and return unused cartons, totes and tools to their defined positions.

title: Restock, rework or scrap decisions
text:
1. Complete inspection in Zone F before recording any restock, rework or scrap decision under PR-07 Returns handling.
2. Assign each returns pallet to returns staff for grading against the customer return reason, physical condition and packaging integrity.
3. Returns staff inspect returns in Zone F and propose restock, rework or scrap for every line on the returns receipt.
4. Propose restock only for sealed, undamaged and fully traceable units that match the system item master and batch requirement.
5. Direct repairable, relabellable or repackable units to rework with a written instruction stating the required action and the target stock location.
6. Propose scrap for contaminated, expired, incomplete or unsaleable units and transfer them immediately to quarantine for write-off control under PR-09 Damaged-goods handling.
7. Present every proposal, with inspection photos and quantity counts, to the shift supervisor for final decision without delay.
8. The shift supervisor approves the final disposition of inspected returns and no restock, rework or scrap move may proceed without that approval.
9. Book approved restock back to its Zone B, Zone C or Zone E location by scanner immediately after approval.
10. Release approved rework units to the rework area in Zone F and return them to inspection on completion before any restock booking.
11. Value every scrap and damaged-goods proposal in EUR at cost price before seeking write-off approval.
12. Obtain shift supervisor approval for damaged-goods write-offs up to 750 EUR and record the approval, value and reason in the system.
13. Escalate damaged-goods write-offs above 750 EUR to the warehouse manager for approval and hold the goods in quarantine until the decision is recorded.
14. The warehouse manager approves damaged-goods write-offs above 750 EUR and no adjustment above that threshold may be posted on shift authority alone.
15. File the inspection record, disposition approval and write-off approval together against the original return authorisation for audit.

Returns staff shall not pre-book restock before inspection is finished. Shift supervisors shall reject incomplete proposals and return them for re-inspection. Warehouse managers shall review recurring scrap reasons at stock reviews and direct corrective replenishment or handling changes where patterns continue.

title: Damaged goods and quarantine
text:
1. Execute PR-09 Damaged-goods handling for every unit found broken, leaking, crushed, contaminated, wet, or otherwise unfit for normal storage or sale.

2. Transfer the affected unit to quarantine on the same shift it is discovered, without waiting for valuation or approval. During storage and returns work, place damaged stock on a pallet or in a containment tray to prevent further spillage.

3. Isolate all quarantine stock physically inside the quarantine area in Zone F. Never leave damaged goods in receiving, bulk, picking, dispatch, or traffic aisles while awaiting a decision.

4. Attach a quarantine tag at the time of transfer. Record the date, time, SKU, quantity, location of discovery, type of damage, name of the discoverer, and pallet identifier where applicable.

5. Enter the quarantine movement in the system immediately after the physical transfer. Keep the stock blocked from sale, replenishment, picking, and dispatch until formally released or written off.

6. Photograph the damage before any repacking or sorting. Retain the photographs with the PR-09 Damaged-goods handling record for audit and claim use.

7. Assess whether partial salvage is possible. Separate intact inner units from destroyed outer packaging only inside Zone F, and return only clean and fully saleable units to the inspection flow.

8. Value the proposed write-off at cost price in EUR. Prepare one write-off request per incident, listing SKU, quantity, unit cost, total value, cause, and attached photographs.

9. Submit write-offs valued up to 750 EUR to the shift supervisor for decision. Do not scrap, destroy, or adjust the system until the shift supervisor approves the write-off.

10. Escalate write-offs valued above 750 EUR to the warehouse manager for decision. Damaged-goods write-offs above 750 EUR need warehouse-manager approval, and system adjustment or destruction must wait for that approval.

11. Respect the accountability structure on every case. The shift supervisor approves damaged-goods write-offs up to 750 EUR, the warehouse manager approves damaged-goods write-offs above 750 EUR, and the warehouse manager is accountable for the whole site: operations, safety and final sign-offs.

12. Carry out the approved outcome without delay. Release salvageable stock through the system, send scrap for destruction through the defined waste route, and file the signed approval with the quarantine log.

13. Review quarantine holdings each working day. Chase overdue valuations, missing photographs, and pending approvals so that no damaged pallet remains in the quarantine area in Zone F longer than operationally necessary.

14. Prohibit unauthorised removal from quarantine. Release stock only on documented approval, and record the name of the approver, the quantity released, and the destination on the PR-09 Damaged-goods handling form.

title: Aisles, walkways and speed limits
text:
1. Apply PR-11 Pedestrian safety in the warehouse on every movement inside the building, in the outdoor yard and on all dock approaches.
2. Drive all handling equipment within the posted limits at all times without exception.
3. Do not exceed 8 km/h inside the building.
Reduce speed early before entering doorways, bends, intersections and areas with restricted visibility, and give way to pedestrians at every crossing.
4. Do not exceed 12 km/h in the outdoor yard.
Adjust speed further for wet surfaces, darkness, glare and yard traffic, and keep to the marked driving lanes.
5. Slow to 5 km/h in marked pedestrian zones and crossings.
Stop where sight lines are blocked, make eye contact with pedestrians before proceeding, and sound the horn where the layout requires it.
6. Do not exceed 5 km/h on dock ramps and leveller approaches.
Approach levellers squarely, check that the leveller plate is seated and secure, and do not mount or cross a leveller showing a fault or warning tag.
7. Use main transport aisles as the primary travel routes for longitudinal movement.
Main transport aisles are 4.0 m wide.
Keep both sides clear of pallets, packaging, chargers and staged equipment, and never park or double-handle loads in them.
8. Enter rack storage aisles only for put-away, replenishment or picking tasks.
Rack storage aisles are 3.0 m wide.
Proceed at walking pace where the aisle is occupied, check both ends before entering, and reverse out only with a banksman or mirrors where rear visibility is limited.
9. Keep segregated pedestrian walkways exclusively for foot traffic.
Segregated pedestrian walkways are 1.2 m wide.
Never place pallets, pallet jacks, waste or tools in walkways, never cut across them with a truck, and cross them only at the marked crossings after slowing to the pedestrian-zone limit.
10. Maintain separation between trucks and pedestrians at interfaces.
Yield to foot traffic at walkway crossings, keep forks low and the load stable when passing, and stop the truck completely when a pedestrian steps into the travel path.
11. Report faded floor markings, damaged barriers, blocked walkways and defective speed signage immediately for repair.
Treat any unmarked or unclear section as a pedestrian area until markings are restored, and operate at the lower speed limit in the meantime.
12. Enforce these limits during congestion, shift changes and peak dispatch activity.
Slow down rather than overtake in narrow sections, queue in the direction of travel, and wait for the aisle to clear before entering with a loaded pallet.

title: Yard, docks and ramps
text:
1. Keep all forklift travel in the outdoor yard at or below 12 km/h.
2. Adjust speed early for congestion, wet surfaces and poor visibility without exceeding the yard limit.
3. Give way to reversing trailers and hold clear of their swing path during manoeuvres.
4. Slow to 5 km/h or less on every dock ramp and leveller approach.
5. Square up to the leveller before crossing and drive straight on and straight off.
6. Stop completely if the leveller plate bounces, sticks or sits unevenly, then report the door for inspection.
7. Never overtake on ramps, at door openings or on leveller approaches.
8. Sound the horn before leaving the building onto the yard and before entering the building from the yard.
9. Serve the building only through its 8 dock doors.
10. Direct inbound receiving traffic to dock doors 1-4.
11. Release outbound dispatch traffic only through dock doors 5-8.
12. Prohibit staging or parking that blocks access to any of the 8 doors.
13. Obtain door and time-slot allocation from the dispatcher before calling a carrier forward.
14. Accept that the dispatcher assigns dock doors and time slots to carriers.
15. Wait for dispatcher confirmation before swapping a trailer between an inbound and an outbound door.
16. Approach the assigned door number only; do not queue at a different door to save time.
17. Confirm the trailer is braked and restrained before positioning a forklift on the leveller.
18. Treat each of the 8 dock doors as equipped with its own dock leveller.
19. Keep the leveller pit and hinge area free of pallets, wrap and debris.
20. Lower and secure the leveller after loading or unloading finishes before the trailer departs.
21. Switch off the forklift and remove the key when leaving the truck unattended in the yard.
22. Park forklifts only in the marked areas clear of dock approaches and trailer turning circles.
23. Keep pedestrians out of active dock approaches and trailer manoeuvring lanes.
24. Apply PR-11 Pedestrian safety in the warehouse to every yard crossing and dock approach.
25. Escort any visitor on foot in the yard and keep to the marked pedestrian routes.
26. Report damaged levellers, doors, bumpers, wheel guides and yard markings for repair without delay.

title: Pedestrian protection and PPE
text:
1. Apply PR-11 Pedestrian safety in the warehouse on every walk through the building and yard. Keep to marked routes, obey barriers and signage, and never take shortcuts through racking or staging areas.

2. Use only the segregated pedestrian walkways for movement on foot between zones. Segregated pedestrian walkways are 1.2 m wide and are marked and physically separated from forklift traffic.

3. Wear a high-visibility vest at all times on the warehouse floor. High-visibility vests are mandatory for everyone on the warehouse floor, including visitors, drivers and office staff entering operational areas.

4. Wear safety footwear class S3 on the warehouse floor. Safety footwear class S3 is mandatory on the warehouse floor and must be fastened correctly before entering Zone A, Zone B, Zone C, Zone D, Zone E or Zone F.

5. Expect forklifts to slow to 5 km/h in marked pedestrian zones and crossings. Make eye contact with the operator before stepping onto a crossing and wait until the truck has stopped or passed.

6. Give priority to pedestrians at every marked crossing. Stop the forklift, lower the forks and allow people to clear the aisle before proceeding at 5 km/h through the marked pedestrian zone.

7. Keep the 1.2 m walkways clear of pallets, stretch film, waste and handling equipment at all times. Report blocked, faded or damaged markings and barriers to the shift supervisor for immediate correction under PR-11 Pedestrian safety in the warehouse.

8. Enforce vest and footwear compliance at zone entries. Challenge any person without a high-visibility vest or safety footwear class S3, stop the task and direct the person off the floor until compliant.

9. Separate pedestrians from manoeuvring trucks at dock ramps, aisle intersections and around the value-added services area. Use pedestrian barriers, mirrors and floor markings to maintain visibility where forklifts operate close to the 1.2 m walkways.

10. Treat every breach of PR-11 Pedestrian safety in the warehouse as a safety incident. Record missing PPE, speeding through crossings or walking outside designated routes, and review the report with the shift team before resuming work.

11. Instruct new starters and visitors in pedestrian protection before unaccompanied access. Explain the 1.2 m walkway system, the 5 km/h limit for forklifts in marked pedestrian zones and crossings, and the mandatory high-visibility vests and safety footwear class S3 on the warehouse floor.

title: Electric fleet overview
text:
1. The site operates an all-electric materials handling fleet supplemented by manual aids and shared dispatch equipment.
2. Forklift operators operate forklifts, reach trucks and pallet jacks.
3. The maintenance technician maintains MHE, racking and dock equipment and logs all repairs.
